title: Quotations for Chapter 19 (the quantity theory and the bullion controversy): Hume's 'Of Money' and 'Of the Balance of Trade' (1752, first edition and a later text); the crisis of 1797, the Restriction and the resumption of 1821 in Cannan's introduction to The Paper Pound (1919), with his Tables I and II; the Bullion Report (1810); Ricardo's High Price of Bullion (1810); Thornton (1802) on the velocity of notes and the Bank's rate of discount; Tooke's History of Prices (1838); Silberling (1919) on the premium on bullion and the Hamburg exchange, with his Tables 6 and 7; Edvinsson (2010) and Fregert (2014) on Sweden's paper standard of 1745-1776
source: D. Hume, Political Discourses (Edinburgh, 1752), first edition on archive.org, and Hume's Political Discourses, ed. W. B. Robertson (Walter Scott, undated), Project Gutenberg eBook 59792; E. Cannan (ed.), The Paper Pound of 1797-1821 (London: P. S. King, 1919), with the Report of the Select Committee on the High Price of Gold Bullion (1810), on archive.org; D. Ricardo, The High Price of Bullion, a Proof of the Depreciation of Bank Notes, 3rd ed. (London: John Murray, 1810), on archive.org; H. Thornton, An Enquiry into the Nature and Effects of the Paper Credit of Great Britain (1802), on archive.org; T. Tooke, A History of Prices, vol. I (1838), on archive.org; N. J. Silberling, 'British Financial Experience 1790-1830', The Review of Economic Statistics 1(4), 1919, JSTOR Early Journal Content on archive.org; R. Edvinsson (2010) and K. Fregert (2014), chapters of Historical Monetary and Financial Statistics for Sweden, vols. I and II (Ekerlids forlag and Sveriges Riksbank), the PDFs on the Riksbank's website
series: id, dynasty (place), year, year_note, value (numbers in the quotation, ';'-separated; fractions as a/b; for the table rows, the column's values for each year in order, an empty field for a year without a value), unit, numeral (unused), file (key of 'sources'), juan (location: printed page, with the PDF page for the image rows), quote (verbatim, as in the document's text, or a transcription for the image rows), note
license: Quotations for criticism and teaching, each with its source. Hume (1752), the Bullion Report (1810), Ricardo (1810), Thornton (1802) and Tooke (1838) are in the public domain; Cannan's introduction (1919) and Silberling (1919) are public-domain publications of 1919 (Silberling's article is in JSTOR's Early Journal Content: 'People may post this content online or redistribute in any way for non-commercial purposes'). The Project Gutenberg text is used under the Project Gutenberg licence (no Project Gutenberg trademark is used here); the archive.org texts are OCR of public-domain scans. Edvinsson (2010) and Fregert (2014) are quoted in short passages from the PDFs that Sveriges riksbank publishes on its website, with the authors, the book and the page. The chapter's Chinese renders the English; the translations are the book's.
fetch: data/fetch/verify_web_quotes.py (rows citing hume_pd, hume1752ed1, cannan1919, ricardo1810, thornton1802, tooke1838, silberling1919, edvinsson2010 and fregert2014; the cannan1919img and silberling1919img rows are read on the page images); checks/check_ch19.py (the readings and every quotation of the text)
notes: Hume. The Gutenberg text (Robertson's edition) is the text of Hume's later editions; the first edition of 1752 (rows h1_*, OCR that reads long s as f, quoted as it reads) differs in the thought experiment of 'Of the Balance of Trade': 'four parts' of the money annihilated and the money 'multiply'd four-fold' (rows h1_fourparts, h1_fourfold), where the later text has 'four-fifths' and 'fivefold' (rows hm_fourfifths, hm_fivefold); both versions say the same thing, and the chapter quotes the later text and gives the first edition's numbers. The later text's 'three-sevenths' (row hm_louis) is 'three fevenths' in the first edition (row h1_louis). Cannan (1919). The OCR text omits the running heads of the odd pages and garbles fractions and some numbers ('51 £ and 57!' for 51¾ and 57¾; '1 80' for 180 (row ci_divisions); '£i' for £1); those passages are read on the page images (rows ci_*), and the text rows quote only what the OCR reads correctly, with the page as printed (introduction in roman numerals, the Report from p. 1). Cannan's Table I gives the public expenditure and revenue of Great Britain and Ireland, their difference, Jevons's index of prices and the Bank of England's commercial bills under discount (from 1795); Table II the Bank's notes in circulation and coin and bullion at the end of February and of August; columns not used here are not transcribed. The Report quotes the Bank's witnesses with a quotation mark at the start of each line; the OCR keeps them and the rows quote them as they read (row br_same) or quote a fragment within a line (rows br_force, br_revert). Ricardo (1810). The passages on cause and effect (rows rc_effect, rc_value, rc_wholly) are in a footnote that runs from p. 15 to p. 16, in which Ricardo answers a passage of 'the work to which I have already alluded'; the third edition is quoted. Tooke (1838). Rows tk_peel and tk_50to100 state views that Tooke reports in order to dispute them: the critics of Peel's bill (that it lowered prices by 30 to 50 per cent, not by the 4 or 5 per cent difference between paper and gold that Ricardo expected), and 'those persons' who ascribe the rise and fall of prices between 1797 and 1814 to the currency; Tooke's own view is that the seasons and the war, not the currency, explain most of the movement (rows tk_theories, tk_erroneous, tk_beyond). Silberling (1919). Table 6 measures the premium on bullion with Spanish silver dollars: the paper price in pence per ounce against the 'theoretical price (gold)', 913.277d. divided by Soetbeer's ratio of gold to silver at Hamburg (rows sb_silver, sb_430, sb_913); the percentage deviation is the premium of the paper price over the gold price. The row for 1813 prints 81.2, 56.2, +23.0 and +40.9: the deviation and the percentage agree with each other (23.0/56.2 = 40.9 per cent) but not with 81.2 (81.2 - 56.2 = 25.0, which would be 44.5 per cent), and Silberling's Chart 3 (p. 288) plots 1813 at about +41; the chapter uses the percentage column, and 81.2 is probably a misprint for 79.2. Table 7 gives the London exchange on Hamburg in schillings Flemish banco per pound, its par (the ratio of gold to silver times 2.3177, row si_par) and the percentage deviation from par. Sweden. Edvinsson's pages (179-184) and Fregert's (342-351) are those printed (the PDF page plus 132 and 338). Edvinsson's notes of 1743 (9.5 million daler silvermynt) rest on another source than Fregert's balance sheet (see riksbank_sweden_1740_1777).
